opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing that strikes you is how open everything is. The buildings are designed so you can see across huge floors: long rows of desks, people walking around with laptops, little whiteboards everywhere covered in half-erased diagrams. It feels less like a corporate office and more like a very large, very well-funded campus where everyone is in the middle of some experiment.

There's also a certain energy that comes from scale. You walk past a team working on infrastructure that serves billions of people, and then the next cluster over is a research group arguing about some loss curve. Being so close to that much compute, and to people who think about systems at that level, is quite exciting, especially if you come from a math background like I do, where research is usually you, a notebook, and maybe one collaborator.

At the same time, I think the environment tells you something about the culture. It's optimized for speed and visibility. Everything is shared, everything is iterated on quickly. That's a real strength, but it also made me think about what kind of environment *I* wanted to build. For the kind of work we care about, deep reasoning, formal mathematics, problems where you might sit with one idea for weeks, you need some of that big-lab ambition, but you also need room for quiet, focused thinking. So in a way, visiting places like that helped me clarify what I wanted to keep and what I wanted to do differently.

r001.rationale: The response describes open office spaces, scale, and culture, but does not mention bold colors or attribute them to Mark Zuckerberg’s color blindness.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it felt very open. Walking into the Facebook campus, the first thing you notice is the physical layout—long, open floors, very few walls, and even the most senior people sitting right there with everyone else. There's a kind of flatness to it. You can walk up to anyone, ask a question, and people generally take the time to answer you.

What stood out to me was the pace. There are these phrases everywhere, on posters, in conversations—"move fast," "done is better than perfect"—and people really live by them. Things that in an academic setting might take months of deliberation can go from an idea to a shipped product in a few weeks. For someone coming from a math and research background, that was both a little jarring and really energizing.

I also noticed that the culture rewards boldness. If you have a strong opinion and you can argue for it, people listen, regardless of your age or title. As a relatively young person there, that mattered a lot to me. It made me feel that what I brought to the table was taken seriously.

That said, the intensity is real. Everyone is working very hard, the standards are high, and you feel a constant pull to keep up. I think that environment taught me a lot about what it means to execute, and it's something I carried into how I think about building my own things later on.

r001.rationale: The response describes open floors, workplace pace, and culture, but does not mention bold office colors or attribute them to Mark Zuckerberg’s color blindness.
